svg.text: VISION v1 · BUILDING A BIGGER DATASET · D1

text.tspan: outlines → masks · semantic, instance and panoptic labels
How the fourteen people of the two photos became labels — and what a bigger dataset’s labels look like.
Every dataset starts with someone drawing the answer
holes where an arm or the legs leave a gap. Tracing is slow — which is why the rest of this section is about getting more out of every label.
: the corner points as traced, and the pixels inside them
, in the photo’s own pixels. Right: the polygon filled —
pixels that now hold the number
. Across both photos a person took
points: more where arms, hands and legs

tspan.style: font-family:'DejaVu Sans Mono', Menlo, Consolas, 'Courier New', monospace;font-size:11.8px;font-weight:600;fill:var(--ink)

text.tspan: each person is one record — the photo, the person’s number, the polygons — the same idea as public datasets, which store an object as a list of polygons and its class.

svg.text: instance: each person their own number

text.tspan: B · Three kinds of segmentation label
what each says about the same photo
a class for every pixel: person or background
what this model learns — all people one colour
the masks with every number above
which object every pixel belongs to: person
counting people, following one person, telling who is in front
both: every object numbered, and every other pixel a class — wall, floor, sky
a full description of the scene
would need wall and floor labelled too

The tracing kept each person’s own number although this model only needs person or background. Labels are the expensive part of a dataset: saved with the most detail they have, they can train a later model that tells people apart (instance segmentation) without tracing anything again. A semantic mask cannot be turned back into
